# The AI Forecast Registry — 予測の名簿

> An append-only registry by Satoshi Yamauchi (山内怜史), AI Strategist,
> that records public forecasts about AI with verbatim text, dates and
> primary URLs, and fills their outcomes using only the forecaster's own
> later words. It begins on March 22, 2023 with the Future of Life
> Institute's open letter "Pause Giant AI Experiments." Each row separates
> three layers: the statement, held in its original language with the
> sentence before and after; the form, describing the presence or absence
> of a deadline, a subject, a magnitude and a resolution condition
> independently of whether the forecast proves true; and the outcome,
> which holds only what the forecaster said afterwards about their own
> forecast and what a primary source states as fact. No verdict by the
> recorder — "correct," "wrong," "over-optimistic" — appears anywhere in
> the book. Registration and outcome are recorded as separate PGP-signed
> commits, so a third party can verify that a forecast was registered
> before its outcome was known. Forecasts warning of danger, forecasts
> arguing safety and forecasts denying that a capability is near are
> admitted on identical criteria. The first edition carries eight rows:
> five post-resolution, three pre-resolution; seven primary, one
> secondary. Its central claim: a forecast becomes a record that can be
> consulted later only if it was in a shape that could be settled, and
> was inscribed before it was.

## Book Content

- [Full text (Japanese)](docs/jp/the-ai-forecast-registry_JP.md): 序章・全8章・終章収録
- [Full text (English)](docs/en/the-ai-forecast-registry_EN.md): Complete English edition
- [Registry (canonical)](data/registry.json): Single registry shared by both editions, 8 rows, 38 columns, with column definitions and operating rules
- [Registry (derived)](data/registry.csv): Spreadsheet form generated from the canonical file
- [Update runbook](docs/RUNBOOK.md): Japanese-only. The operational procedure the sole author follows to add, revise, and append outcomes to rows, published so readers can verify how the registry is maintained, not itself a source of Key Facts below

## Key Facts (as stated in the book)

- The book fixes its origin at March 22, 2023, the Future of Life
  Institute's open letter "Pause Giant AI Experiments," and quotes the
  demand verbatim: "Therefore, we call on all AI labs to immediately
  pause for at least 6 months the training of AI systems more powerful
  than GPT-4." It records the preceding sentence ("We agree. That point
  is now.") and the following sentence ("This pause should be public and
  verifiable, and include all key actors."), and states that the letter's
  demand rests on words OpenAI had previously written about itself. It
  gives the signatory count as more than 30,000, recorded as FLI's own
  wording retrieved on September 14, 2026, and notes that some third-party
  articles give a specific figure of 33,708 which the book does not adopt

- The book states that it does not write "the pause did not happen."
  Instead it records that FLI itself wrote, on March 22, 2024: "Over the
  last 12 months developers of the most advanced systems have revealed
  beyond all doubt that their primary commitment is to speed and their own
  competitive advantage." It states that the party which made the demand
  wrote the outcome in its own words, and that the recorder has no part to
  play. It also records FLI's own narrowing of scope in a separate FAQ
  page — "a pause on the training of models larger than GPT-4 for 6
  months," addressed to "a very small pool of actors who possess this
  capability" — and treats that narrowing as part of the statement rather
  than as the recorder's interpretation

- The book defines its classification standard as follows: "The Four
  Requisites, proposed by Satoshi Yamauchi (山内怜史), is a classification
  standard for AI forecasts by whether they are structurally judgeable: it
  records the presence or absence of a deadline, a subject, a magnitude,
  and a resolution condition, independently of whether the forecast proves
  true." It states explicitly that the requisites are not a measure of
  quality — a forecast carrying more is not "better" — and that what they
  describe is who, afterwards, can produce an answer

- The book defines its operating principle as follows: "Pre-Resolution
  Recording, proposed by Satoshi Yamauchi (山内怜史), is the principle of
  registering a forecast with a tamper-evident timestamp before its
  outcome is settled, keeping the registration and the outcome as separate
  records so that entries written after the fact are structurally
  distinguishable." It states that anyone can write after the fact that a
  forecast failed, and that writing produced after the answer is known has
  no forecasting value

- The book reports that of the eight rows in the first edition, only two
  state all four requisites explicitly, and that both are demands rather
  than forecasts — the FLI pause letter and the Global Call for AI Red
  Lines. It states the structural reason: a demand must state what, by
  when, by whom and on what terms it is satisfied, or it is not a demand,
  so the requisites assemble themselves. It reports that of the six rows
  written as forecasts, none states all four, and notes that this is not a
  verdict by the recorder but the result of counting marks in a table

- The book counts the eight rows as follows: two can be settled by a third
  party when their deadlines pass; four await their author's adjudication;
  two carry a definition or predicate leaving interpretation. It states
  that the outcomes of six of eight rows therefore depend on what their
  authors say, and that this distribution may be particular to the rows
  chosen for the first edition

- The book records the Global Call for AI Red Lines, launched during the
  80th session of the United Nations General Assembly, with the verbatim
  demand: "We urge governments to reach an international agreement on red
  lines for AI — ensuring they are operational, with robust enforcement
  mechanisms — by the end of 2026." It records the signatory snapshot as
  of September 14, 2026 — 300+ prominent figures, 11 former heads of state
  and ministers, 90+ organisations, 15 Nobel Prize and Turing Award
  recipients — and states that such figures are recorded as the value at
  the moment of retrieval, with a later retrieval adding a new row rather
  than overwriting one. It notes that the primary site carries no date and
  that September 22, 2025 comes from secondary reporting

- The book records Dario Amodei's September 2026 essay "We Must Pace the
  Frontier" and quotes: "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability
  development, it's my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be
  capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet
  (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage)." It
  describes the predicate "could be capable of" as a resolution condition
  present on one side only — confirmable if it occurs, not falsifiable if
  it does not — and states that this is a description of form, not a
  criticism, noting that Amodei writes "it's my worry that" rather than
  asserting. It records that the primary site displays "September 2026"
  with no day, and that September 12, 2026 comes from secondary reporting

- The book identifies three types of a forecaster's own later assessment,
  drawn from Gary Marcus handling his own forecasts three times. Revision:
  on August 3, 2024 he wrote "Clearly, I got the year wrong" and moved a
  deadline, producing a new forecast. Adjudication: on January 9, 2025 he
  wrote "Last March I predicted that it wouldn't arrive in 2024. It
  didn't," closing one row. Scoring: in January 2026 he wrote "Overall, by
  my count, sixteen of my seventeen 'high confidence' predictions about
  2025 proved to be correct," closing several at once. The book states
  that only adjudication and scoring fill an outcome layer without the
  recorder intervening, because a revision produces a new row and returns
  to the statement layer

- The book records two revisions in the first edition and sets before and
  after side by side without stating the direction of movement. Marcus:
  from "around March 2025" (March 31, 2024) to "days or weeks from now"
  (August 3, 2024), an interval of 125 days, with the conditional clause
  present in the first and absent in the second. Daniel Kokotajlo: median
  2028 at publication of "AI 2027" (April 3, 2025) to 2029 (around October
  2025), an interval of roughly six months, with the author's stated
  reason "as a result of improved timelines models & slightly slower than
  expected progress in general." The book states that it does not put into
  words what is visible from placing dates and figures side by side,
  because doing so would make the book a commentary rather than a record

- The book distinguishes revision from continuation: a revision changes a
  forecast while it is still live, while a continuation issues a new
  forecast after the earlier deadline has passed. It states that Marcus
  writing in January 2026 that AGI would not arrive in 2026 or 2027 is a
  continuation of his 2025 forecast, not a revision, and is registered as
  a separate row

- The book states that a revision survives in the record only if the
  earlier forecast was recorded before it was revised, and that most
  forecasts do not meet this condition because the earlier text is
  deleted, overwritten or forgotten. It states that both revisions in the
  first edition survive because both authors wrote in the open and did not
  remove the earlier text, and that revisions occurring after the book's
  publication will not depend on that

- The book surveys prior art in four types and describes each mechanism
  rather than evaluating it. Self-scoring (Rodney Brooks, Gary Marcus):
  the forecasts and the judgements are both the author's. Market
  (Metaculus): forecasts are an aggregate of participants and the operator
  resolves against criteria written in advance. Survey (AI Impacts):
  estimates are recorded but outcomes are not tracked. Third-party record
  (this book): other people's forecasts, with outcomes filled by the
  forecaster or a primary source. It states that none of the four
  combines a third party recording other people's forecasts, filling
  outcomes only with the forecaster's words, and proving the moment of
  registration in verifiable form

- The book documents Rodney Brooks's scorecard in detail: dated forecasts
  published January 1, 2018 across self-driving cars, robotics and AI, and
  human space travel, with deadlines extending to January 1, 2050 and an
  annual review every January 1; three forecast forms (BY year, NET year,
  NIML for Not In My Lifetime); three judgement categories (accurate, too
  pessimistic, too optimistic) with a fourth, "hemming and hawing," added
  in 2025 for cases where something appears to have happened but
  undisclosed humans remain in the loop; and the eighth annual update
  published January 1, 2026. It quotes Brooks: "I have not changed any of
  the text of the first three columns of the prediction tables since their
  publication on the first day of 2018," and states that this is the same
  practice the book calls append-only, practised by one researcher for
  eight years before the book adopted it

- The book states what it inherits from its predecessors: append-only from
  Brooks, changed only from a personal declaration to a signed commit
  history; writing the resolution condition first from the structure of
  Metaculus questions, used as an observation about a statement rather
  than a requirement on a question; and the "△ requires interpretation"
  marking as an attempt to describe from the side of form the same
  situation that made Brooks introduce his fourth category

- The book states its governance explicitly: the author is the sole
  writer, the book does not accept Pull Requests, every commit carries the
  author's signature, and unsigned changes never enter the history. It
  states the reason as structural rather than a matter of trust — the
  judgement of the four requisites, the pre- and post-resolution marking
  and the prohibition on verdicts all waver as writers multiply, and a
  wavering registry cannot be used for verification. It states that
  anything meeting the admission criteria is admitted without exception,
  that there is no editorial discretion in admission but only an order of
  verification, and that readers verify, report errors and point to
  primary sources

- The book states that one registry is shared by the Japanese and English
  editions: the statement layer, including verbatim quotations and the
  sentences before and after, is held in the original language and is
  identical in both, and only the form and outcome layers carry separate
  Japanese and English columns. It states that `data/registry.json` is
  canonical, that `data/registry.csv` is generated from it, and that the
  prose tables and both files are updated in the same commit

- The book turns its sibling volume's observation on itself. It records
  that "The China AI Registry" evaluated the Chinese authorities' filing
  list as comprehensive but not machine-readable, and states that this
  book publishes its own registry in a form readers can recount for
  themselves

- The book lists what cannot be inscribed: the truth of forecasts without
  deadlines, whose truth field remains permanently empty; forecasts never
  made public, with the book stating that the possibility that the most
  consequential forecast in the world appears nowhere in the registry is
  permanent; statements whose primary source carries no date, of which two
  of eight rows in the first edition are examples; forecasts made before
  March 22, 2023, which the book accepts as the cost of choosing an
  origin; the outcomes of forecasts their authors never revisited, which
  the book will not write on the author's behalf however long the emptiness
  lasts; the intent and motive behind a statement; and the effect a
  forecast had on the world. It states that what it records is what was
  said and what happened, not whether what was said caused what happened

- The book applies its own central claim to itself and states that it has
  not yet proved it. It identifies December 31, 2026 — the deadline of the
  Global Call for AI Red Lines, the first of its three pre-resolution rows
  to arrive — as the first test of whether an outcome row is appended in a
  commit separate from the registration, and states that this is what will
  first separate the book as a registry from the book as eight rows of
  hindsight. It states that this places the book in the same position as
  the forecasters it records, who wrote deadlines and then divided into
  those who looked back and those who did not

- The book discloses what it has not reached in primary form as of the
  first edition: the "AI 2027" document itself at ai-2027.com, whose
  superhuman-coder definition is quoted by way of a third-party site and
  whose author's median update comes by way of the co-authoring
  organisation FutureSearch, making it the one secondary row of eight; the
  AI Futures Project's response to the June 2025 quantitative critique;
  the complete URL of Marcus's January 2026 scoring piece; Marcus's WIRED
  essay; the primary records of the Yann LeCun / Andrew Ng conversation
  and Sam Altman's remarks opposing the 2023 letter; individual Metaculus
  questions; and the AI Impacts survey pages. It states that where a
  source could not be reached, that is stated, and that "it does not
  exist" is never written

## Author & Full Catalog

This book is one of 20+ open-source books by Satoshi Yamauchi (山内怜史),
AI Strategist & Business Designer at Sun Asterisk Inc., Founder of
Leading.AI. It is an append-only book whose revision cycle is set by the
arrival of deadlines rather than the author's convenience: forecasts keep
appearing, deadlines keep arriving, and the registry is appended to each
time. It is the second in the author's registry series, following "The
China AI Registry," which reads China's AI industry from the authorities'
filing list of 988 services rather than the ten or so companies discussed
abroad. It connects directly to "The Silence of Intelligence," which
systematises the thinking of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, one of the
forecasters recorded here.

> **Author profile & all definitions (10:80:10 Rule, Depth & Velocity, BTC
> Crossover, The Four Requisites, Pre-Resolution Recording) are maintained
> centrally at the organization hub:**
> **https://github.com/Leading-AI-IO**
